taskTitle: Twelve HTTP status codes, by the book

checks.detail: 0 state changes, each allowed by a review (0 reviews in all)
1 phase had the tools designed for them

finalText:
I've got all twelve definitions and am now putting together the answer.

All twelve codes are defined in RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), the current specification, at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html. It has a general list of heuristically cacheable codes: "Responses with status codes that are defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification)…". It adds that "all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable."

**Heuristically cacheable:**
- 203 Non-Authoritative Information (15.3.4)
- 206 Partial Content (15.3.7)
- 308 Permanent Redirect (15.4.9)
- 405 Method Not Allowed (15.5.6)
- 410 Gone (15.5.11)
- 414 URI Too Long (15.5.15)
- 501 Not Implemented (15.6.2)

Each of these sections says so in its own text. For 206, the spec says the default can be overridden only by explicit cache controls. For the others, it can be overridden by the method definition or by explicit cache controls.

**Not heuristically cacheable:**
- 303 See Other (15.4.4)
- 307 Temporary Redirect (15.4.8)
- 413 Content Too Large (15.5.14)
- 421 Misdirected Request (15.5.20)
- 422 Unprocessable Content (15.5.21)

None of these sections says they are cacheable, and none appears in the list above.

I found no conflicts between sources; everything comes from that one page. In the quotes below, line breaks from the RFC's plain-text layout are shown as single spaces.
